fatal_errors: The proposed high-pressure/high-temperature processing intervention is unrelated to the target thermal-aging comparison at approximately 600°C and 750°C.

The hypothesis invokes conventional grain-boundary segregation and decohesion, whereas the target mechanism is ordering- and phase-boundary-mediated plastic instability involving L12-ordered FCC domains and jagged B2/FCC boundaries.
It predicts only generic toughness degradation and misses the decisive non-monotonic ductile-brittle-ductile transition.
The stated high- and low-temperature boundaries are undefined and conflict with cited cryogenic evidence showing enhanced rather than degraded toughness.
The assumed single-phase baseline does not represent the target as-cast FCC+B2 eutectic microstructure.
explanation: The response addresses toughness degradation in compositionally complex alloys and proposes a testable grain-boundary mechanism that has limited support from E7, so it is a scientifically plausible alternative rather than wholly unsupported. However, it largely repeats the conventional-alloy expectation that the prompt asks the comparison to distinguish. It does not reconstruct the alloy, aging window, L12 ordering, jagged FCC/B2 phase boundaries, elevated antiphase-boundary energy, planar slip, phase-boundary crack initiation, or recovery through reduced ordering and ductile transition zones. The proposed experiment could test whether deliberately segregated boundaries reduce toughness, but it is underspecified, changes segregation and precipitation simultaneously, and lacks the spatially resolved dislocation/crack-initiation measurements needed to distinguish grain-boundary decohesion from phase-boundary plastic instability. Most cited evidence is irrelevant to the claimed mechanism; only E7 offers meaningful support, while the cryogenic studies undermine the broad low-temperature degradation claim.
